The surah opens by glorifying God: dominion is in His hand and He has power over all things. Most commentators explain "tabaraka" as exalted and abundant in good, while others take it to mean enduring or holy above all attributes ascribed to Him. As for "the dominion," al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others understand it as sovereignty over the heavens and earth in this world and the next. Ibn Ishaq relates it to the prophetic kingship through which God honours His followers and humbles His opponents. All agree that "the hand" stands for power and control, not a bodily organ.

The commentators also agree that God created death and life to test people and see which of them acts best. Qatada saw death as a humbling of the children of Adam, with this world a place of life and passing and the hereafter a place of recompense and permanence. Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan read "best in deed" as the most detached from this world, while Fudayl ibn Iyad understood it as the most sincere and most in line with the Sunna. Some reports describe death as a ram and life as a mare, but not all scholars accept these accounts as reliable.

The surah then describes the seven heavens placed one above another. Most commentators understand "tafawut" as flaw, inconsistency or crookedness, and "futur" as cracks or breaches. Repeated looking is meant to bring the eye back defeated and exhausted, finding no fault. The stars, in the majority view, adorn the lowest heaven, serve to pelt the devils and guide people, while the devils will face the blazing fire in the hereafter.

The commentators explain that the verse displays God's absolute power and complete sovereignty, for He created death and life in order to test people and see which of them does the best deed, and it closes with the names al-'Aziz and al-Ghafur. Most agree that the deed must be sincere, done for God alone, and in accordance with the Sunna, and that the verse encourages obedience and warns against disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir report, through a tradition attributed to the Prophet, that the best deed is that of the one with the most sound intellect, the most scrupulous about what God has forbidden, and the swiftest in obedience; al-Hasan, al-Thawri, and another report from Ibn 'Abbas take it to mean the one most detached from this world, while al-Suddi understands it as the one who remembers death most and prepares for it best. Regarding death and life, most scholars, including al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, hold that death is an existent attribute opposed to life, and Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi describe symbolic forms of death as a ram and of life as a mare, which several scholars treat as an image rather than a literal fact. Muqatil also explains death as the drop of semen and life as the breathing in of the spirit. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan treat the interrogative clause as a suspended construction, a view debated among grammarians. Death is mentioned first, according to most, because it is more effective in spurring good action or because it is closer to divine subjugation.

The verse describes God who created seven heavens layered one above another, and invites the observer to look at the creation of the Most Merciful and find no flaw in it. The commentators agree that the verse denies any discord in the creation of the heavens, and that the observer must repeat his gaze until he is certain, seeing no crack, so that his sight returns humbled and worn out. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take this reading. On the word tibaq, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as the heavens lying one above another, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss several grammatical analyses, since the word may be a verbal noun meaning correspondence or the plural of tabaq. On the meaning of tafawut, Qatada and Ibn Abbas understand divergence or dispersal, al-Suddi a defect, and Ibn Qutayba and al-Baghawi irregularity and dissonance, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya understand a lack of proportion. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and others read tafawwut with a doubled consonant, the rest tafawut, and al-Tabari considers both readings to have the same meaning. On futur, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it to mean cracks, Qatada a gap and Ibn Abbas a weakness. Al-Tabari explains that repeating the gaze means multiplying it, and the commentators agree in rendering khasi'an as humbled and hasir as exhausted and tired. Some modern commentators read here a mutual attraction between heavenly bodies, but this reading was not adopted by most classical exegetes.

This verse describes the flawless creation of the seven heavens layered above one another. Whoever looks at them finds no disproportion, defect or crack. He is told to look again and again, and his gaze will return to him humbled and exhausted, having found nothing. The commentators agree on the central point that the Creator's work is without fault, and that the repetition demanded means careful and sustained reflection rather than exactly two glances. On the meaning of tafawut, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Ibn Abbas, take it as divergence or inconsistency, Qatada as discord, and al-Suddi as a defect, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi relate it to the root fawt, meaning that one part fails to fit another. For futur, Mujahid and al-Dahhak understand cracks, Qatada a flaw, and al-Suddi breaches. For khasi'an, Ibn Abbas says humbled, Qatada says abased, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Akhfash say distanced, like a dog driven away. Hasir means worn out, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi observe that the dual form expresses repetition rather than the number two. Al-Tabari reports that some held khasi'an and hasir to have the same meaning. Ibn al-Qayyim links the absence of disproportion to the Creator's will, and Ibn Kathir adds that the stars serve as adornment, as missiles against devils, and as guides. Several works also cite hadiths on the merits of Surat al-Mulk, but these reports do not bear directly on the meaning of the verse.

This verse states that God adorned the nearest heaven, the lowest sky, with lamps, which the commentators understand as the stars and planets that shine at night, and that He made them projectiles against the devils, while preparing for them in the Hereafter the torment of the Blaze. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take the lamps to be the stars, and most commentators agree that their role as adornment does not require them to stay fixed in place. Following the image of a torch taken from a fire that remains burning, Zamakhshari, Razi and Nasafi explain that the shooting stars are flames separated from the stars' fire, which themselves stay unchanged. Most identify the targeted devils as jinn who try to eavesdrop on the angels. Zamakhshari, Razi and Qurtubi also report an interpretation in which the projectiles are guesses hurled at astrologers, a sense Tabari and Ibn Kathir do not adopt, treating it as a secondary reading. Qatada holds that the stars were created for three purposes: adorning the sky, striking the devils, and guiding travellers, and that whoever assigns them other functions has spoken without knowledge, a view widely repeated by Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy. As for the Blaze, Ibn Abbas places it at the fourth level of Hell, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Alusi note that a fire stronger than the jinn's own fire can harm them. Razi records the views of earlier philosophers on the nature of meteors and answers their objections without settling the matter definitively.

This part of the verse announces that those who disbelieve in their Lord will face the punishment of Hell, which is an evil destination. The commentators explain that it comes after the mention of the punishment of the devils and extends the warning to all disbelievers, among humans and jinn alike, so that no one thinks the threat concerns only the stoned devils. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir agree that the destination named is Hell itself, and that describing it as evil conveys blame and a warning. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word Jahannam may first refer to the uppermost level of the fire and then to all its levels, and he takes it here to mean Hell in its entirety. In a reading reported from al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and others, the word 'adhab is in the accusative, which links it to 'adhab al-sa'ir; al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud cite this variant. Al-Razi and al-Alusi observe that the exclusive sense is relative, since other texts describe the punishment of sinners, so the verse cannot be used to claim that only disbelievers are punished. Ibn 'Ashur sees the sentence as a completion aimed at the mass of polytheists. The verses that follow then describe the roar and the boiling of the fire.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers when they are cast into Hell: they hear from it a chahīq, a dreadful and repulsive sound like the braying of a donkey, while it seethes and boils (tafūr) with them as a cauldron boils with its contents. The commentators agree on the basic meaning: the chahīq is a fearful, loud cry. They differ on who makes it. The more common reading, held by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and others, attributes the cry to Hell itself, which lets out a gasp toward them, whereas al-Mawardi reports that it may also be the cries of the damned themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi describe the chahīq as a loud cry, and al-Razi gives several possibilities: the roar of the Fire, the cries of those cast in earlier, or the cries of the damned. On the difference between chahīq and zafīr, al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani report that the first is the beginning of a donkey's bray and the second its end, a view al-Sam'ani favours. Mujahid and Ibn Mas'ud compare the boiling to a pot or to grains in a large amount of water. Al-Razi and al-Alusi explain the anger attributed to the Fire as a figure of speech, while al-Shinqiti holds that the Qur'an truly grants the Fire a form of perception and wrath. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the passage a metaphor for the violence of the flames.

This verse describes Hell when the disbelievers are thrown into it: it is nearly torn apart by its fury against them. Each time a group is cast in, its keepers ask them a question of rebuke: did no warner come to you? The people admit that a warner came, but they denied him and said that God had sent down nothing, and that the messengers were in great error. The commentators agree that 'tamayyaz' means to split apart or break up, and that the 'ghayz' here is intense anger against the wrongdoers, as Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd explained, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr read it as being cut off, and some took it to mean boiling. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the question is a reproach meant to add to their punishment and their regret. Opinions differ on who speaks the words 'you are only in great error': al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take them as the disbelievers' words to the prophets, whereas al-Zamakhshari, and al-Razi as an alternative, allow that the keepers may be speaking. Mujahid held that the warners were jinn and the messengers humans, a view al-Sam'ani rejects as unsound, and most scholars take the warner to be a human messenger. Several scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, draw from the verse that God punishes only after a warning has come, and that the disbelievers acknowledge God's justice. Their admission 'had we listened or reasoned' is read by the commentators as regret for having neither listened nor reflected.

This verse describes what the inhabitants of Hell face when they are cast into it: its keepers ask them, as a rebuke, whether no warner came to them. They admit that a warner came, but say they denied him and claimed that God had revealed nothing, and that the messengers were in grave error. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand these words as spoken by the damned to the messengers, while al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan report that most commentators take them as the disbelievers' words to their warners. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud note that the words could also be spoken by the keepers to the disbelievers, or be quoted from the messengers in the world, while al-Alusi finds these last options strained. All agree that the damned acknowledge God's justice, that the sending of messengers removed every excuse, and that their rejection brought their punishment. They also agree on the meaning of their confession of guilt, explained by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi explain that the word for error may mean ruin itself or the punishment for error. The damned then say that had they listened or reasoned, they would not be among the people of the Blaze. Al-Zamakhshari notes that hearing and reason are joined because religious responsibility rests on both, and al-Razi draws from this an argument for the superiority of hearing over sight. Al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi report the view that no one is punished before a messenger has come.

This verse reports the words of the people of the Fire when they admit their failure: had they listened to the truth with the attentiveness of one who reflects and seeks guidance, or understood it with the reason of one who reasons and discerns, they would not be among the companions of the Blaze. The commentators explain that the hearing and reason meant are those that benefit from guidance; the disbeliever is treated as having no useful hearing or reason, since he did not profit from them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that this is a confession made too late, to which the response is the invocation «fasuhqan», meaning distance or remoteness. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the readings with the ḥā' vowelled or unvowelled are two dialectal forms of the same word, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih report that suhq is a valley in Hell. Ibn 'Abbas understands it as listening to guidance in order to act on it, while al-Zajjaj takes it as the hearing of one who understands and the reason of one who discerns. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi link hearing and reason because religious obligation rests on both; al-Razi adds that hearing comes before reflection. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that sins weaken the intellect. Some exegetes drew theological arguments or a ranking of hearing over sight from the verse, a point al-Alusi mentions without deciding.

This passage describes the admission of the people of the Fire, who acknowledge their sin when they are questioned about the messengers, and then a curse is pronounced upon them: far away from God's mercy. The commentators agree that this confession brings them no benefit at that moment, and that the word suhqan is a supplication of distance, placed in the accusative as the object of an implied verb. Most readers pronounce the ḥā' with a sukun, while Abu Ja'far and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma; both are accepted as two dialects of the same word. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih report that suhq is the name of a valley in Hell, while Ibn 'Abbas also understands it simply as distance. Al-Tabari explains that the singular dhanb is used with a collective sense, as in the expression 'ata' al-nas. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya stress that confessing and denying are equally useless at that stage. Ibn Kathir reports that the damned admit they had neither hearing nor reason to guide them. The commentators draw no legal rulings from this verse.

This verse states that those who fear their Lord in the unseen, that is, when they are away from people's eyes, will receive forgiveness and a great reward, which is Paradise, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'the unseen'. Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliya and al-Sudi take it to be what is hidden from them, namely God, the angels, Paradise and Hell. Zirr ibn Hubaysh takes it to be the Quran, Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid takes it to be Islam because it is absent from sight, and Yahya ibn Salam takes it to be the moment of solitude when a person remembers his sin and seeks forgiveness. Others, such as Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that it means piety in private, and Ibn Juzayy considers both readings possible. Al-Razi notes that one who fears God in secret fears Him all the more in public. The following verses tell people to keep their speech secret or make it public, since God knows what the breasts conceal, and then remind them that He made the earth submissive so that they may walk in its paths and eat of His provision, and that the resurrection is to Him. Scholars also differ on the word 'manakib': Ibn Abbas and Qatada say the mountains, Mujahid says the roads and passes, al-Kalbi and al-Farra' say the sides and regions, and al-Tabari prefers the regions and extremities. The commentators agree that the promise to believers follows the warning to the disbelievers.

This verse teaches that God knows what people whisper and what they say openly, so that secrecy and openness are the same to Him, since He knows what the hearts contain. The commentators relate that, according to Ibn Abbas, some polytheists of Mecca told one another to speak quietly so that Muhammad's God would not hear them, and the verse answers them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the verse as a call to watchfulness over one's conduct even when alone, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the man who gave charity in secret among those shaded by God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress that the secret and the open are equal in God's knowledge. Al-Razi draws a rational argument from the phrase "Should not He who created know?", holding that whoever creates a thing must know it, and he uses this to argue against the Mu'tazilite view that people create their own acts. Grammarians differ over whether "man" in "Should not He who created know" is the subject or the object, which changes the meaning slightly. Al-Qurtubi notes that the imperative form here conveys a statement of fact, and several commentators link the verse to God's subtle kindness toward His servants.

In this verse God declares that His knowledge encompasses everything people conceal, since the One who created them cannot be unaware of what they hide. He is the Subtle, the All-Aware. The commentators agree that the question is a rebuke and a denial that God could be ignorant of this. They differ, however, on the grammar of "man khalaqa". Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others take it as the subject of the verb, with the object understood as the hidden thoughts or the secret and the open speech. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as the object, with God as the subject, meaning that He would not know His own creation. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di prefer the first reading, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim stress that creation implies knowledge and see the verse as a proof that God creates what is in the heart. Al-Qurtubi relates a story of a man who heard this verse in a grove at night. On the meaning of "al-Latif", al-Razi reports views that it means the knower of subtleties or the One who acts in ways hidden from most agents, while Ibn 'Ashur links it to knowledge of hidden matters and gentle management. "Al-Khabir" refers to the One whose knowledge misses no hidden event. Several commentators note that the verse answers unbelievers who whispered, thinking the Prophet could not hear them. The surrounding verses also link the fear of God in private with forgiveness and a great reward.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls God's favour in making the earth docile, meaning gentle and easy, so that people can walk upon it, settle on it and benefit from it. They are therefore told to walk through its sides and regions in search of provision, to eat of the sustenance God gives, and to remember that they will all be raised back to Him. Most exegetes agree on this general meaning. They differ, however, on the word manakib. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the mountains, while al-Farra', al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Qutayba understand it as the sides and regions. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Tabari favour roads, passes and extremities, and al-Tabari concludes in favour of regions, by analogy with the shoulders of a person, which are their outer parts. Az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi read the phrase as an image of extreme submissiveness, since the shoulder of a camel is its most delicate part, which no rider would tread upon. Al-Hasan understands provision as what is lawful, while others take it as what God causes to grow. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn al-Qayyim regard the command as a permission accompanied by a blessing, with eating meaning benefiting in general, and they see in it an encouragement to work and to seek means, without contradicting reliance on God. Sayyid Qutb reads it as an invitation to reflect on the laws of creation.

This verse asks the disbelievers whether they feel safe from what Allah, who is above the heavens, could do: cause the earth to sink beneath them so that it shakes and moves violently until they perish. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, relying on Ibn Abbas, take 'He who is in the heaven' to mean Allah Himself, or His power, authority or punishment. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi mention another reading, that it refers to the angels or to Gabriel, who is charged with punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that the wording may follow the belief of the Arabs, who placed God in the sky. Khasf means the earth sinking downward, as it did to Qarun, and mawr means shaking and moving back and forth. The hasib is either a rain of stones or a wind carrying pebbles. The passage then turns to birds spreading and folding their wings, held aloft only by the Most Merciful, to prompt reflection on God's power. Ibn Juzayy, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Sa'di see the verse as a warning meant to frighten the disbelievers, whose outcome would be dire. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur, who dwell on the literal meaning of 'in the heaven', treat it as an ambiguous (mutashabih) expression and consider both interpretation and the approach of the early scholars, who left the meaning undefined, as valid options.

This verse rebukes the disbelievers for feeling secure. They are asked whether they feel safe from the One in the heaven, who could cause the earth to swallow them so that it shakes and sways beneath them, or send against them a hasib, a violent wind carrying stones or pebbles, so that they will learn how true His warning was. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand the phrase to refer to God Himself, although al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn read it as the punishment of the One in heaven. Al-Zamakhshari gives two explanations: that it refers to God's dominion, with His throne and angels in heaven, or that it follows the disbelievers' own belief that mercy and punishment come down from above. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also mention the view that it refers to angels, or to Gabriel according to al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud. On the meaning of the hasib, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir define it as wind with stones, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi add the view that it is a cloud with stones, and al-Qurtubi cites the destruction of the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant. Most commentators read nadhir as the act of warning, while Ata, al-Dahhak and al-Razi take it as referring to the Prophet. The passage then recalls earlier nations who denied their messengers and the birds that spread and fold their wings, kept aloft only by the Most Merciful, as al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari explain. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri emphasise the warning and the power and mercy of God.

This verse states that the peoples who denied their messengers before the Quraysh, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, faced God's rejection and punishment, which was severe and terrible. It is both a warning to the polytheists of Mecca and a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ. The commentators link it to the preceding threat of being swallowed by the earth or struck by a storm of stones: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi recall that God destroyed some nations by engulfment, such as Qarun, and others by stones, such as the people of Lot. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain nakir as God's disapproval and punishment, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi emphasise the dreadful nature of that chastisement. On the phrase 'He who is in the heaven', al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Sa'di understand it as God's power exalted above all creation, al-Mawardi also reports the view that it refers to the angels, and al-Tha'alibi notes that verses about divine elevation must be understood without assigning God a place. The passage then turns to the birds spreading and folding their wings, which only the Most Merciful keeps aloft; al-Razi sees in this a proof of divine power. Readers differ over whether the letter ya is written in 'nadhiri' and 'nakiri', a matter of orthography that does not change the meaning. Overall, the fate of past nations is a sign to be heeded.

In this verse God directs the disbelievers to a sign they see every day: birds spreading their wings in flight and then folding them. Most commentators agree that only the All-Merciful holds them up in the air, meaning by His power and by the form He gave them, with bodies and feathers suited to gliding through the air. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abbas place the verse within the warning of the earth being swallowed up and of a shower of stones, while Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn al-Qayyim treat it mainly as a call to reflection. The commentators agree on the meaning of 'saffat' (wings spread) and 'yaqbidna' (folding them). Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Razi and al-Alusi explain why the noun is used for spreading, the basic state of flight, and the verb for folding, which happens from time to time. Al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi add that without this power the weight of the birds would bring them down. Ibn Sa'di stresses the lesson of this sight, which is to recognise God's oneness. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan reject any naturalist reading, whereas Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse an argument based on the subtlety of flight. All agree that God encompasses everything with His knowledge and His sight.

God addresses the Meccan polytheists with a rhetorical question of rebuke and denial: who is the army that will help you and defend you apart from the Most Merciful, if He wills harm for you? The commentators explain that there is no helper for them except God, and that the disbelievers are only in a delusion that the devil has placed in them, making them think that punishment will not reach them and that their idols benefit them and bring them near to God. There is broad agreement that the verse denies any support or provision coming from anyone other than God. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'jund' means a force and a helper, and that 'lajju fi 'utuw wa nufur' means persisting in error, obstinacy and turning away from the truth. Al-Zamakhshari suggests the pronoun may refer to all the idols, which the pagans believe protect them and provide for them. Al-Razi reports that the disbelievers relied on two things, their strength and wealth, and on their idols, and that the verse refutes both. Ibn al-Qayyim, citing a narration attributed to Wahb ibn Munabbih, concludes that God alone suffices His servant, supports him and provides for him. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the question is meant to show that no one can be named as such a helper. The commentators link this passage to the preceding verses about the threat of being swallowed by the earth or struck by stones, and to the birds that spread and fold their wings by the sole power of the Merciful. Ibn Juzayy and al-Jalalayn add that the disbelievers' delusion lies in believing themselves safe.

This verse says that God alone provides sustenance: if He withheld His provision, no one else could bring it to people. Despite this clear truth, the disbelievers persisted in obstinacy, arrogance and turning away from the truth. The commentators agree on the main sense: it is a rebuke based on a fact no reasonable person can deny. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain 'utuww as rebellion and transgression, and Mujahid explains nufur as disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand it more as a stubborn persistence in hostility and a flight from what is true, which weighs heavily on them. Al-Razi links the arrogance to attachment to worldly gain and the aversion to ignorance. On the meaning of rizq, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Mahalli take it to be rain, while al-Qurtubi, al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Ashur extend it to all the goods of this life. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi suggest that the word 'this' may refer to the idols that the pagans believed protected and provided for them, whereas others treat it as a hypothetical case. Ibn al-Qayyim connects the verse to the theme of divine help, and al-Shinqiti notes that the power to create implies the power to provide. These scholars link the passage to the verses about birds and the earth, all of which are signs of God's power.

This verse poses a comparison: who is better guided, the one who walks hunched and stumbling with his face to the ground, or the one who walks upright on a straight path? The commentators treat it as a rhetorical question whose answer is obvious. They largely agree on the core meaning: the disbeliever, blind to the truth, is like someone who keeps falling, while the believer, who sees clearly, walks with confidence.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak take the parable as a general image of the believer and the disbeliever in this life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi hold that it describes the disbeliever who was bent over his sins and will be gathered on his face on the Day of Resurrection, as Qatada says, and they cite the hadith of Anas about God's power to make people walk on their faces. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi add that the hunched walker may also be a blind man who cannot find his way. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi discuss the grammar of the verb akabba, and Abu Hayyan explains that mukiban is a state. Ibn 'Ashur reads the image as a metaphor for the crooked road of idolatry against the straight path of Islam.

Some reports name specific people: Abu Jahl for the one who walks bent, and the Prophet, Hamza or Ammar ibn Yasir for the one who walks upright, as recorded by al-Sam'ani, al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi. Ibn Juzayy and al-Jalalayn keep to the general sense of the parable. Across the classical and modern commentaries, the central point is the same: uprightness on a clear path is guidance.

This verse states that God created human beings and gave them hearing, sight and hearts, and that their gratitude for these gifts is very small. The commentators differ on what this smallness means. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean that people barely give thanks at all, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur read it as a rhetorical way of denying gratitude altogether, comparing it to saying that a land rarely produces a certain crop. Al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani say that smallness means complete absence. Al-Razi explains that the gifts were wasted by not being directed toward God's pleasure, and al-Biqa'i notes that hearing, sight and hearts are named for understanding.

The verse belongs to a larger argument against the polytheists. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri point out that no idol can provide sustenance or victory, and that the disbelievers persist in arrogance. Several commentators, including al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari, read the image of a man walking face-down as a parable of the disbeliever and that of a man walking upright as the believer, while Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima and others name specific people such as Abu Jahl, Hamza or Ammar. Ibn Kathir adds that people will be gathered on their faces on the Day of Resurrection.

The verse then recalls that God scattered humanity across the earth and that all will be gathered back to Him. The disbelievers ask when this promise will be fulfilled. The Prophet replies that knowledge of the hour belongs to God alone and that he is only a clear warner. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the promise to be the Resurrection, while Mujahid takes the sight from nearby to be the punishment of Badr. Most readers take the word tadda'una to mean claiming or asserting, while others read it as calling upon God, as in the request for punishment.

This verse means that God is the One who brought you into being and scattered you across the earth, and that you will be gathered back to Him alone for reckoning and recompense. Most commentators read the verb dhara'a as creating, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti do, and as Ibn Abbas is reported to say. Ibn al-Jawzi, however, relays from Ibn Shajara that it means spreading people out and dispersing them over the earth's surface, a view al-Qurtubi also records. Al-Mawardi offers a third possibility: that God made you to grow on the earth until your formation was complete and your term ended. The word hashr, gathering, refers to resurrection after death, according to al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir. Al-Razi links the verse to the proofs of divine power given just before it: the power to create at the start implies the power to recreate, which is why gathering follows creation. The commentators agree that the verse answers disbelievers who denied resurrection and demanded to know when it would occur. The next verse replies that knowledge of the hour belongs to God and the Prophet is only a clear warner. Al-Razi explains this by distinguishing knowing that the event will happen from knowing when it will happen, and Ibn Sa'di adds that truth is recognised through its proofs rather than through knowing the date. No legal ruling is raised in this verse; the disagreement concerns the meaning of the verb dhara'a.

This verse reports the question of the unbelievers who deny the resurrection: they ask, mockingly and impatiently, when this promise will come, if you are truthful. The commentators understand the promise as the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, though al-Razi notes that some take it to mean punishment in general. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi read it as a sarcastic question addressed to the Prophet and the believers, expressing denial. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya connect it to what precedes, where God recalls the gifts of hearing, sight and hearts and the gathering to Him, which makes the question more provocative.

The exegetes agree on the answer given in the next verse: knowledge of the hour belongs to God alone, and the Prophet is only a clear warner. Ibn Sa'di stresses that truthfulness is recognised by its proofs rather than by a fixed date, and that demanding a date is injustice and stubbornness. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the question is mockery, and that the word "promise" is used to demand its fulfilment.

They differ on the meaning of the promise, which may be the Last Day or punishment in general, and on whom the address "if you are truthful" targets, the Prophet and the believers or others. On the word tadda'un, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari read it as claiming or demanding, while al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba take it as asking or calling for, and Qatada reads it as urging the punishment to come faster.

God tells His Prophet to say to the pagans who deny resurrection and press for the Hour that knowledge of its timing belongs to God alone, and that he himself is only a clear warner who conveys what he has been commanded. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take the promise to mean the gathering and the punishment, which the disbelievers asked about, saying when it would come. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur distinguish between knowing that the promise will be fulfilled, which the Prophet knows and which suffices for warning, and knowing its exact time, which is not part of the warner's role. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan read the verse against a background of mockery, since the disbelievers demanded a fixed date and hastened the punishment, and Abu Hayyan adds that they wished for the Prophet's destruction. Ibn Sa'di notes that the demand for a date is wrongly taken as a test of truthfulness, since truth is known through evidence. The commentators agree on the general sense, which closes a series of arguments about God's power over creation and resurrection. They differ only on what the promise refers to and on the punishment the disbelievers will see close at hand: the punishment of the Hereafter, as most say, or the punishment of Badr, as Mujahid reports.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers when they see the promised punishment close at hand: their faces are darkened with sorrow and gloom, and they are told, as a rebuke, that this is what they used to demand be hastened. The commentators agree that the pronoun refers to the promise of punishment, and that the word zulfa means near or present. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani take it to mean nearness or direct sight, al-Hasan understands it as direct witnessing, and Ibn Zayd as presence. As for their faces being marred, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi explain it as blackening and sorrow covering them, while al-Zajjaj says the evil became visible on their faces as a sign of their disbelief. The scholars differ on what the promised punishment is. Most, such as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that it is the punishment of the Hereafter, whereas Mujahid identifies it with the punishment of Badr; Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani also mention the nearby gathering. Those who speak the rebuke are, according to most, the guardians of Hell, as Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi state, though some say the disbelievers address one another. On the meaning of tadda'un, two readings prevail: the majority, including al-Farra', al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, take it as asking for or calling for the punishment to be hastened, whereas al-Zajjaj, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi read it as claiming, that is, denying the resurrection. The reading of Ya'qub and Qatada without the doubled letter is reported by al-Tabari as meaning the request for punishment. Taken together, the verse portrays the disbelievers recognising the reality they had denied, and being humiliated and filled with regret.

God commands His Prophet to answer the idolaters who wished for his death and the death of his companions. He says to them: if God destroys us, or grants us mercy, who will protect the disbelievers from painful punishment? According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Jalalayn, neither the death nor the survival of the believers saves the disbelievers from God's punishment, and they should repent and return to faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the believers are waiting for one of two good outcomes, death as martyrs leading to Paradise or victory, while the disbelievers remain in constant danger. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi stress that the disbelievers will have no protector whatever happens. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer another reading: the believers themselves fear their sins and hover between fear and hope, so the disbelievers, who have no hope, are in a worse state. The commentators agree that the following verses contrast the believers' faith and trust in God with the clear error of the disbelievers. Some report the context: the Meccans were calling for the Prophet's destruction or plotting to kill him and his followers. The differences concern mainly the vowelling of the pronouns in 'ahlakani' and 'ma'iya', and whether 'fasa-ta'lamun' is read in the second or third person, which does not greatly change the overall meaning.

God commands His Prophet to tell the polytheists who wish for his destruction and that of his companions: He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him and we have put our trust in Him, and you will soon know who is in manifest error. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the believers affirmed the Most Merciful and entrusted their affairs to Him, while the disbelievers will not be saved by the Prophet's death or survival. The commentators agree that the verse is a threat that ends with certain knowledge at the moment the punishment is witnessed. Most report that the passage answers their wish to see the Prophet perish. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that placing belief before reliance hints at the disbelievers, and that placing the object of reliance first signals exclusivity: trust in God alone, not in men or wealth. On recitation, al-Kisa'i reads the verb in the third person, while the others read it in the second person. No legal ruling is drawn from the verse, and the commentators do not differ on its general meaning, only on certain details of wording.

God tells His Prophet to ask the polytheists: tell me, if your water sinks so deep into the earth that buckets cannot reach it, who will bring you flowing water visible to the eye? The commentators explain that the question aims to remind the Meccans of the blessing of water and to make them acknowledge that only God brings it. The word ghawr means water that has sunk into the ground, and ma'in means water that is apparent and flowing. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari report that the water meant is that of the well of Zamzam and the well of Maymun, so the verse warns the people of Mecca about losing their supply. On the meaning of ma'in, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' take it as sweet water, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr as pure water, and Qatada and others as running water. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the word may mean abundant or visible to the eye, and do not choose between them. Ibn Kathir stresses that only God makes water spring forth and flow. Many commentators link the verse to the preceding challenge to those who wished for the death of the Prophet and the believers: salvation comes neither from their destruction nor from mercy alone, but from faith and reliance on God. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi also relate that a mocker who heard the verse said that axes and hoes would bring the water, and he lost the sight of his eyes; they cite it as a warning.
